chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Salih, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: Verily, God — Mighty and Majestic — has, in every night of the Month of Ramadan, those who are freed and released from the Fire, except for the one who breaks his fast with an intoxicant. And when it is the last night of it, He liberates in it the like of what He liberated during the whole of it.

key_terms.طُلَقَاء: Those released/pardoned; emphasizes the idea of voluntary release, distinct from manumission
key_terms.عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: Mighty and Majestic — an honorific used when mentioning God's name
key_terms.عُتَقَاء: Those freed from bondage (of the Fire); plural of 'atiq
key_terms.مُسْكِر: Any intoxicant; substance that causes loss of reason; broadly haram in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about God liberating people from hellfire during Ramadan?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches that God grants freedom from Hellfire to believers every night of Ramadan, a divine mercy that accumulates throughout the month. The final night carries an even greater reward — God frees souls equal in number to all those freed during the entire month combined. However, this mercy is withheld from those who break their fast with intoxicants, connecting the spiritual opportunity of Ramadan with the obligation to maintain ritual purity during fasting. The hadith reflects how early Shia audiences understood Ramadan not merely as physical abstention but as a period of divine clemency and spiritual liberation.
